newsitem.title: USA: CEO pay rises while companies downsize - report.
newsitem.headline: CEO pay rises while companies downsize - report.

text.p: Thousands lost jobs at major companies across the United States last year as executives at many of those companies enjoyed heftier compensation packages, according to a study released Thursday.
"CEOs should be rewarded for creating good jobs -- not destroying them," said John Cavanagh, co-director of the non-profit, liberal Institute for Public Policy and one of the authors of the study.
"These CEOs claim they have to lay people off to strengthen their businesses," he said. "But we are sceptical when all the compensation savings go into the CEO's pocket."

The gap between the pay of chief executive officers and employees widened as the average U.S. worker received a 3 percent raise in wages in 1996, the Institute for Policy Studies said in its fourth annual executive compensation survey.

American workers' compensation gains slowed in the first three months of 1997 as slower-growing benefit costs moderated a pick-up in wages and salaries, the Labour Department said in its quarterly Employment Cost Index on Monday.
The study by Cavanagh and institute fellow Sarah Anderson examined 30 domestic companies that reported layoffs ranging from 2,800 to 48,640 workers.
In the last quarter of 1996, layoffs totalled 459,000 workers, up 2 percent from the final quarter of 1995.

According to the study, AT&T Corp. led the "downsizing pack" with an announcement of 49,000 layoffs. However, Chairman Robert Allen took a 14 percent pay cut for 1996, largely due to lackluster stock performance.
AT&T's 1997 proxy statement, issued April 1, put Allen's 1996 compensation package at $5.5 million, down from $6.4 million and contained no stock options or restricted stock grants.

According to the institute study, CEOs at the 30 companies that reported layoffs saw total direct compensation -- consisting of salary, bonus and long-term compensation such as stock options -- rise 67.3 percent, well above the average increase of 54 percent for executives at the top 365 U.S. companies.
Most of the increased earnings came in the form of gains from stock options, "reflecting the continued trend on Wall Street to reward downsizers," the study asserted.
Recent shareholder initiatives enhanced incentives for the CEOs to cut jobs by pressuring companies to tie more and more of CEO pay to performance, the study said.
The share of CEO total pay in the form of salary has been shrinking, while bonuses and stock options have risen.
A 1996 institute study calculated that CEOs from the 22 largest job-cutting companies enjoyed a combined increase in the value of their stock options of $37 million the day they announced the layoff.
